doc.title: Ray Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Opinions on today's jazz radio, blues and new age
summary: He finds KLON's blues and contemporary smooth jazz monotonous background music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Any current jazz people that you—
Well I was just going to say, we get — do you know KLON?

Yes. In Long Beach State College. And the jazz station, they play all day long and night, 24 hours, and they’re I guess on the satellite and they go all over the country. Every time I turn them on they’re playing the blues.

So you know I was so happy that — I live out in the desert, the high desert, and gee we’ve got cable, and which we got cable FM along with it. And then they got KLON on the cable, oh this is great. I’ll be able to hear what guys are doing. I think it’s the most accessible kind of jazz you know, blues. I don’t know what other excuse they have. I’m too general, but enough that I don’t even turn it on. And then of course what’s considered jazz today, whatever they call new age jazz or contemporary, on the Black Entertainment Channel they had a series and I guess it’s still on but it’s not on at the same time, where they did like contemporary — whatever they call contemporary. I think it’s gotten to be, it took the place of new age really. Because the WAVE, what is it, in L.A., I think plays that kind of stuff now, and that was originally a new age place. And the guys are great, the players, but I think it’s just background music, that’s what people use it for. And to © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-
me it gets monotonous after a while. It’s like we used to call “mood music.” And it’s just not interesting to me. I admire the performer, but just sit down for fun.
It’s almost the Mantovani of the 90s.
Yeah. I’m hopeful it isn’t that bad yet. And guys, what the heck, they’re making a good living at it.
